query: High-entropy alloys can combine mechanical strength, wear resistance, corrosion protection, oxidation resistance, and thermal stability, while their large compositional space offers opportunities to tune degradation in harsh environments. Prior studies have largely considered wear and corrosion separately, and only a few reports address their combined action, leaving the governing behavior poorly understood. For a high-entropy alloy subjected to tribo-corrosion, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs the coupled response and why? Describe a controlled comparison that would isolate the governing cause, predict changes in total degradation and its wear and corrosion components relative to a matched baseline, state where the prediction should hold or fail, connect it to the available prior evidence, and identify a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The coupled tribocorrosion response in HEAs is governed by the balance between wear-induced removal and in situ regeneration of a protective, noble-element‐enriched oxide film; when mechanical wear exposes the less-protected matrix at heterogeneous phase boundaries, micro‐galvanic interactions accelerate localized corrosion, so that the net degradation is determined by how fast the passivating layer is removed versus how rapidly it reforms.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy with a dual-phase microstructure—comprising a primary BCC matrix and secondary phases that preferentially enrich corrosively inert (noble) elements leading to the formation of a stable passivating oxide film.
generation.intervention: Impose controlled tribological sliding in a corrosive environment (e.g., 3.5 wt% NaCl solution) both on as-prepared HEA surfaces and on surfaces pre-oxidized to develop a stable oxide layer.
generation.conditions: Ambient to moderate temperatures where oxide formation kinetics allow regeneration (but not so high as to inhibit film formation), using identical wear testing conditions (e.g., pin-on-disk) combined with electrochemical monitoring.
generation.structural_mediator: The microstructural heterogeneity—specifically, the secondary phase regions that form the noble-element–rich passivating film, and their interfaces with the more reactive BCC matrix that serve as micro-galvanic couples.
generation.mechanism: Mechanical wear locally removes the protective oxide film, exposing the reactive underlying metal and creating micro-galvanic sites at phase boundaries; in parallel, the alloy’s passivation kinetics work to reform the protective layer. The net tribocorrosion behavior thus results from the competition between continual film removal by wear and film reformation that protects against corrosion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a baseline HEA with an intact passivating surface, samples experiencing aggressive wear will manifest increased localized corrosion (and thus higher total degradation) due to recurrent oxide removal. In contrast, samples with a pre-established, robust oxide layer should exhibit reduced wear-accelerated corrosion, diminishing overall degradation rates.
generation.baseline: HEA samples exposed to quiescent, low-wear conditions where the passivating oxide film remains largely intact, resulting in lower overall degradation (both wear and corrosion) rates.
generation.boundary: This prediction holds in regimes where the rates of mechanical wear and oxide reformation are comparable. It may fail under extreme wear conditions that remove the oxide layer faster than it can regenerate, or in environments (e.g., very high temperatures or highly reactive media) where oxide film formation is inhibited.
generation.uncertainty: The exact kinetics of oxide film removal and regeneration are not precisely known and may vary with specific alloy composition and microstructural distribution; additionally, the quantitative impact of micro-galvanic coupling at phase boundaries is uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA samples: one set with surfaces pre-oxidized to establish a robust passivating layer and a second set with mechanically polished, oxide-free surfaces. Subject both sets to identical tribological sliding in a 3.5 wt% NaCl solution while continuously monitoring mass loss, corrosion potential, and surface film characteristics using in situ spectroscopy and scanning Kelvin probe microscopy.
measurements: Electrochemical corrosion rate (e.g., via potentiodynamic polarization)
Surface oxide film thickness and composition (using spectroscopy/SEM-EDS)
Mapping of surface potential variations (using scanning Kelvin probe)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-oxidized samples do not exhibit significantly lower localized corrosion rates and overall degradation compared to the oxide-free samples—i.e., if protective film presence does not correlate with reduced tribocorrosion damage—the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract WVTaTiCr x ( x = 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1) refractory high-entropy alloy coatings were prepared on a 42-CrMo steel plate using laser cladding. The purpose of this work is to investigate the effect of the Cr content on the microstructure and properties of the WVTaTiCr x coating. The morphologies and phase compositions of five coatings with different Cr contents were comparatively observed. In addition, the hardness and high-temperature oxidation resistance of the coatings were also analyzed. As a result, with the increase in Cr, the coating grains were more refined. All the coating is mainly composed of the BCC solid-solution phase, which promotes the precipitation of the Laves phase with the increase in Cr. The addition of Cr greatly improves the hardness, high-temperature oxidation resistance and corrosion resistance of the coating. The WVTaTiCr (Cr 1 ) exhibited superior mechanical properties, especially in terms of its exceptional hardness, high-temperature oxidation resistance and outstanding corrosion resistance. Abstract Dual-phase high entropy alloys have recently attracted widespread attention as advanced structural materials due to their unique microstructure, excellent mechanical properties, and corrosion resistance. However, their molten salt corrosion behavior has not been reported, which is critical in evaluating their application merit in the areas of concentrating solar power and nuclear energy. Here, the molten salt corrosion behavior of AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was evaluated in molten NaCl-KCl-MgCl 2 salt at 450 °C and 650 °C in comparison to conventional duplex stainless steel 2205 (DS2205). The EHEA showed a significantly lower corrosion rate of ~1 mm/year at 450 °C compared to ~8 mm/year for DS2205. Similarly, EHEA showed a lower corrosion rate of ~9 mm/year at 650 °C compared to ~20 mm/year for DS2205. There was selective dissolution of the body-centered cubic phase in both the alloys, B2 in AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 and α-Ferrite in DS2205. This was attributed to micro-galvanic coupling between the two phases in each alloy that was measured in terms of Volta potential difference using a scanning kelvin probe.
